front: How did WWI impact Germany?
p1: British naval blockade caused mass starvation — 750,000 civilian deaths.
p2: 2 million German soldiers killed; war trebled government debts.
p3: Collapse of law and order - Kiel Mutiny saw sailors refusing to follow orders.

front: What happened in November 1918?
p1: Kaiser Wilhelm had lost control over the army and there was a collapse of law and order by late 1918.
p2: Wilhelm abdicated 9 November 1918; Weimar Republic declared the same day by leading politicians.
p3: Armistice signed 11 November 1918 — no Allied soldier had entered Germany, so many Germans refused to believe they were losing.

front: How did the Weimar Republic begin?
p1: Ebert emerged as dominant politician Nov 1918–Jul 1919, reassuring the army and industrialists that communism would not take hold.
p2: Defeated the Spartacist uprising, proving he could maintain order.
p3: Weimar Constitution agreed July 1919: President (head of state, elected every 7 years), Chancellor (day-to-day government), Reichstag (directly elected parliament).

front: What happened during the Spartacist Revolt?
p1: January 1919: communist Spartacists led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht attempted to seize power.
p2: 100,000 workers struck in Berlin and seized government communication offices.
p3: Ebert sent in Freikorps (far-right ex-soldiers) who crushed the revolt; Luxemburg and Liebknecht were killed.

front: What happened during the Kapp Putsch?
p1: March 1920: Ebert tried to disband the Freikorps; Wolfgang Kapp led 5,000 armed men in a march on Berlin.
p2: Government fled to Stuttgart and called for passive resistance — workers went on strike.
p3: Kapp could not govern and fled after four days; rebellion collapsed.

front: What were the weaknesses of the Weimar Constitution?
p1: Article 48 allowed laws to be passed without the Reichstag in an emergency.
p2: Proportional representation meant it was hard for one party to control government. Led to 9 unstable coalition governments 1919–23.
p3: The Weimar Republic was created out of violence in the aftermath of WWI. Violence was always seen as an acceptable part of politics in Germany.

front: What were the strengths of the Weimar Constitution?
p1: All men and women had equal voting rights.
p2: Power was divided between the President, Chancellor, and Reichstag to avoid one person having too much power.
p3: Proportional Representation meant that everyone's vote had equal weight unlike in the First Past the Post systems of Britain or America.

front: What were the terms of the Treaty of Versailles?
p1: Army limited to 100,000 men; no air force; navy severely restricted. Rhineland on border with France demilitarised.
p2: Germany lost 13% of land including Alsace-Lorraine (to France), all colonies, and the Polish Corridor.
p3: War Guilt Clause (Article 231) forced Germany to accept 100% of the blame for WWI. Had to pay £6.6 billion reparations.

front: How did Germans react to the Treaty of Versailles?
p1: Treaty condemned as a Diktat — Germany had no say in the negotiations led by Wilson, Clemenceau and Lloyd George.
p2: Signatories of the armistice accused of stabbing Germany in the back (Dolchstoss); called 'November Criminals'.
p3: Matthias Erzberger, who signed the armistice, was assassinated by a right-wing extremist in 1921.

front: What caused Hyperinflation?
p1: December 1922: Germany missed a reparations payment; France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr in retaliation.
p2: German government called a general strike in the Ruhr; loss of production caused shortages and unemployment.
p3: Government printed money to pay striking workers, causing a vicious cycle of inflation — a loaf of bread cost 1 mark in 1919 and 200,000 billion marks by 1923.

front: What was the impact of Hyperinflation?
p1: Collapse of society; mass shortages as foreign suppliers refused to accept German marks. People cannot afford basic goods.
p2: Middle-class savings wiped out overnight. Pensions also become worthless.
p3: Loss of trust in the Weimar government, which was seen as unable to manage the economy. Hitler attempted Munich Putsch during Hyperinflation.

front: How did Stresemann stabilise Germany's economy?
p1: 1923: Rentenmark introduced to replace the worthless mark and end hyperinflation. Later strengthened to Reichsmark.
p2: 1924: Dawes Plan — reparations reduced to £50 million/year; USA began $2.5 billion in loans to Germany.
p3: 1929: Young Plan reduced total reparations to £2 billion and extended the deadline to 1988.

front: How did Stresemann improve Germany's foreign relations?
p1: 1925: Locarno Pact — France left the Ruhr; improved relations with Britain and France.
p2: 1926: Germany admitted to the League of Nations — accepted back into the international community.
p3: 1928: Kellogg-Briand Pact — 61 nations agreed to renounce war as a tool of foreign policy.

front: How stable was the Weimar Republic between 1924–1928?
p1: Support for extremist parties dropped from 40% in 1924 to 28% in 1928 as the economy recovered.
p2: Election of war hero Paul von Hindenburg as President in 1925 increased nationalist support for the republic.
p3: But German economy dangerously reliant on American loans; underlying mistrust of government remained.

front: How did life change for workers in Weimar Germany?
p1: Unemployment benefit and sickness benefit introduced for the first time in 1927.
p2: Average working week fell from 50 to 46 hours; wages rose 25% by late 1920s.
p3: Government built 100,000 new homes to ease housing shortage; 4% unemployment rate by 1924.

front: How did life change for women in Weimar Germany?
p1: Women gained equal voting rights; made up 10% of the Reichstag.
p2: Some traditional male jobs opened to women; number of female doctors doubled to 5,000 by 1932.
p3: Women paid on average 33% less than men; the 'new woman' challenged gendered social norms.

front: What was culture like in Weimar Germany?
p1: Berlin became the centre of European avant-garde art and culture in the 1920s.
p2: Architecture: Bauhaus movement. Film: Fritz Lang's Metropolis; stardom of Marlene Dietrich.
p3: Art: Otto Dix painted expressionist works highly critical of German society.

front: How did Hitler join the Nazi Party?
p1: After WWI Hitler was employed as a military spy to investigate the German Workers' Party (DAP) in Munich, run by Anton Drexler.
p2: Hitler became attracted to the DAP's ideas and joined in 1919.
p3: Within two years Hitler had taken control of the DAP and transformed it into the Nazi Party (NSDAP).

front: How did Hitler take over the Nazi party?
p1: 25 Point Programme (1920): campaigned against Weimar politicians, democracy, Jews, Treaty of Versailles and capitalism.
p2: Created party structure: permanent Munich office, swastika logo, Volkischer Beobachter newspaper; brought in Hess, Göring, Streicher, Röhm.
p3: August 1921: formed the SA (Sturmabteilung) — brownshirted ex-soldiers who intimidated opposition with violence.

front: Why did Hitler attempt the Munich Putsch in 1923?
p1: Nazi Party had grown to 50,000 members by 1923; Hitler believed right-wing Bavarian politicians like von Kahr would support him.
p2: Inspired by Mussolini's fascist March on Rome in 1922; boosted by support of war hero Ludendorff.
p3: 1923 context: Ruhr occupation and hyperinflation made Weimar Republic deeply unpopular — moment seemed right.

front: What happened during the Munich Putsch?
p1: 8 November 1923: Hitler and 600 SA burst into a Munich beer hall, fired a gun, and announced his intention to march on Berlin.
p2: Ludendorff mistakenly allowed von Kahr to leave; Kahr alerted the government in Berlin.
p3: 9 November: army crushed the Putsch; 16 Nazis killed. Hitler arrested.

front: What was the aftermath of the Munich Putsch?
p1: Nazi Party and SA banned; Hitler sentenced to 5 years in Landsberg Castle (released after 10 months).
p2: Hitler used his defence speech to gain national publicity; wrote Mein Kampf in prison outlining Nazi ideology.
p3: Hitler concluded direct revolution had failed — decided to win power through elections instead.

front: How did the Nazis reorganise in the 1920s?
p1: Party ban lifted 1925; spread nationwide — each region (Gau) led by a Gauleiter.
p2: SA grew to 400,000 by 1930; Hitler established personal bodyguard (SS) led by Heinrich Himmler.
p3: 1926 Bamberg Conference: Hitler redirected party to far-right nationalism, abandoned socialist policies; won over Goebbels.

front: Why did the Nazis not gain much support in 1924–29?
p1: Stresemann's economic recovery restored faith in Weimar — only 2.6% of the vote in 1928.
p2: Germany's improved international standing (League of Nations, Locarno) cut support for nationalist parties.
p3: Election of Hindenburg as President in 1925 increased support for the republic among nationalists.

front: What was the impact of the Wall St. Crash (1929) on Germany?
p1: US loans recalled immediately; German banks ran out of money and demanded businesses repay loans.
p2: Mass unemployment: 6 million unemployed by 1933 — 50% of all people aged 16–30.
p3: Savings lost in banking crisis; homelessness surged; 24% increase in theft in Berlin.

front: How did the Great Depression affect the Nazis?
p1: Nazis rose from 2.6% (1928) to 37% of the vote and 230 seats by July 1932 — largest party in Reichstag.
p2: Economic desperation drove millions to extremist ideas - Weimar was failing to deal with the crisis so support for moderates collapsed.
p3: Communists (KPD) also became popular - terrifyed the wealthy who bankrolled the Nazis as their only hope.

front: How did the Nazis use propaganda to gain support 1929–32?
p1: Goebbels ran 120 newspapers; ensured Nazi message spread via radio and eye-catching posters across Germany.
p2: Hitler held rallies across Germany, travelling to 5 cities in one day by plane — projected image of a modern saviour.
p3: Nazi policies had broad appeal: 'Work and Bread' for workers; anti-communism for the middle class; protection of land for farmers.

front: Why did Hindenburg make Hitler Chancellor?
p1: Chancellor Brüning resigned May 1932; Hitler was head of largest party but Hindenburg refused to make him Chancellor.
p2: Hindenburg appointed von Papen and then von Schleicher - both failed to control Reichstag without Nazi support. Von Schleicher threatened military dictatorship.
p3: January 1933: von Papen convinced Hindenburg to make Hitler Chancellor with von Papen as Vice Chancellor, believing Hitler could be a mouse in his pocket. Hindenburg reluctantly agreed.

front: How did the Reichstag Fire increase Hitler's power?
p1: 27 February 1933: Reichstag set fire by Dutch communist Marinus van der Lubbe.
p2: Hitler convinced Hindenburg to declare a state of emergency — Decree for the Protection of People and State gave Hitler power to imprison opponents and ban communist newspapers.
p3: 4,000 communists arrested that night. 81 communists removed from Reichstag giving Nazis 2/3 majority.

front: How did the Enabling Act increase Hitler's power?
p1: March 1933 election: campaign of fear and SA violence; Nazis won 288 seats; Hitler had 2/3 majority - enough to change constitution.
p2: Enabling Act passed: give Hitler right to make laws without the Reichstag - end of Weimar democarcy.
p3: Hitler used Enabling Act to ban Trade Unions, all other political parties and local governments (länder).

front: Why was Hitler worried about Ernst Röhm's power in 1934?
p1: Röhm commanded 3 million SA men loyal to him personally — a dangerous rival power base. Röhm publically critical of Hitler.
p2: Röhm favoured a socialist direction opposed to Hitler's policies; the army leadership felt threatened by the SA.
p3: The violent SA made Nazis look like thugs; SS leaders Himmler and Heydrich resented Röhm and wanted him removed.

front: How did the Night of the Long Knives increase Hitler's power?
p1: 30 June 1934: Röhm and approximately 400 other critics within the Nazi Party were murdered.
p2: Other enemies are removed including Von Kahr and Strasser who had crossed Hitler in 1920s.
p3: After Night of Long Knives, no one else in Nazi party would dare oppose Hitler - creates deterrence.

front: How did the death of Hindenburg increase Hitler's power?
p1: 2 August 1934: Hindenburg died aged 87.
p2: Hitler declared himself Führer — combining the roles of Chancellor and President. 90% approved in a referendum.
p3: The army swore a personal oath of loyalty to Hitler, not the republic — power was now absolute.

front: How did the Nazis use the police state to maintain power?
p1: The SS: 300,000 members led by Heinrich Himmler. Had almost unlimited power in Germany. Would send opponents to the Nazis to the feared Concentration Camps like Dachau.
p2: The Gestapo – Secret police ran by Reinhard Heydrich. Relied on a network of informers. 30,000 agents but rumours spread there was one on every corner. SD also listened in on peoples' phonecalls.
p3: All courts and police had to be completely loyal to Hitler. Most serious cases were tried at the People's Court with no jury and no right to appeal. 534 were sentenced to death by 1939.

front: How was propaganda used in Nazi Germany?
p1: Goebbels controlled all radio; People's Radio (cheap, 70% of households) blocked foreign stations. Mass Nuremberg rallies staged annually with 200,000 people and 20,000 flags.
p2: Film used to promote Nazi messages — Leni Riefenstahl directed Triumph of the Will glorifying Hitler.
p3: Berlin Olympics 1936 used as a global propaganda showcase; Germany topped the medal table.

front: How was censorship used in Nazi Germany?
p1: Newspapers regularly briefed on permitted content; hostile papers shut down.
p2: 2,500 writers banned; millions of books removed from libraries and publicly burned.
p3: Jazz banned; Jewish composers like Mendelssohn forbidden; focus on German classical music — Beethoven, Bach, Wagner.

front: How did the Nazis control religion?
p1: Reich Church (1936): Protestant pastors had to support Hitler's views; Mein Kampf and the Bible used in sermons; swastikas displayed in churches.
p2: July 1933 Concordat with Pope Pius XI: Catholic priests would not be political; Hitler would not interfere with Catholic schools (he later did anyway).
p3: Pope publicly criticised Hitler in 1937; Catholic schools brought into line with Nazi schools; Catholic priests harassed and arrested throughout the 1930s.

front: How did young people oppose the Nazis?
p1: Edelweiss Pirates: working-class teenagers who wore long hair and American styles, fought Hitler Youth in the streets, mocked Nazis in the countryside.
p2: Swing Youth: wealthy teenagers who played jazz, owned record players, admired American culture; Himmler ordered them to be beaten and given hard labour.
p3: Opposition was limited — no direct political action, small numbers, motives mainly cultural rather than political.

front: How did priests oppose the Nazis?
p1: Pastors' Emergency League set up by Martin Niemöller — opposed unification of the Reich Church and attempts to stop Jews converting to Christianity.
p2: Confessing Church: 6,000 pastors joined in opposition to Nazi interference; 2,000 remained in the Reich Church.
p3: Opposition largely crushed: 800 priests sent to camps; Niemöller arrested for treason in 1937 and sent to a concentration camp.

front: Did ordinary Germans conform with the Nazis?
p1: Most Germans outwardly conformed due to fear of the Gestapo and social pressure — one informer could destroy a family.
p2: Many genuinely supported Hitler, especially after economic recovery and style national events like the 1936 Olympics.
p3: Private dissent existed — SD reports noted complaints about falling wages and food shortages — but open resistance was rare and dangerous.

front: What were the Nazis' aims about women?
p1: Strongly opposed the 'new woman' of the Weimar era — smoking, drinking, androgynous fashion.
p2: Believed women's role was the 3 Ks: Kinder (children), Küche (kitchen), Kirche (church).
p3: Aimed to reverse women's entry into the workforce and increase the German birth rate to build a 1,000-year Reich.

front: What were Nazi policies towards women?
p1: Law for the Encouragement of Marriage (1933): loans of 1,000 marks to couples who married — only if women stopped work; quarter written off per child born.
p2: Mother's Cross: encouraged childbirth (4 children=bronze, 6=silver, 8=gold); Hitler Youth saluted gold medallists.
p3: Job restrictions - 1933: women banned from being teachers, doctors, civil servants. 1936: no woman could be a judge or lawyer. By 1937 reversed — women pushed back into factories for war preparation.

front: How did the Nazis change education?
p1: 1933: teachers had to swear loyalty to Hitler and join the Nazi Teachers' League; lessons began with 'Heil Hitler' salute.
p2: Curriculum altered: race studies compulsory; PE 4 hours a day; history textbooks rewritten to promote Dolchstoss myth and anti-Semitism; Mein Kampf compulsory.
p3: Girls taught cooking and needlework; all textbooks approved by the Nazis; 1933 — teachers who didn't comply could be sacked.

front: What was the purpose of Nazi Youth Groups?
p1: Hitler Youth (10–18 boys): political, physical and military training — camping, shooting, political education; compulsory from 1939 after only 25% attending in 1938.
p2: League of German Maidens (10–21 girls): same political and physical training but military replaced with housework and racial hygiene.
p3: All other youth groups banned; aim was to create loyal, physically strong Nazis who would sustain the 1,000-year Reich beyond Hitler's lifetime.

front: How did the Nazis reduce unemployment?
p1: German Labour Service (RAD, 1933): paid public work schemes. Compulsory from 1935 for 6 months for all young men. 7,000km of Autobahn (motorway) miles built.
p2: Rearmament: defied ToV — 1.36 million men in army by 1939; arms factories producing tanks, aircraft and guns created mass employment.
p3: Unofficial unemployment hidden by excluding women, Jews and part-time workers from statistics.

front: How did KdF, DAF, and SdA affect German workers?
p1: DAF (German Labour Front): replaced trade unions; workers lost right to negotiate pay; DAF could punish workers who disrupted production.
p2: KdF (Strength through Joy): provided leisure — cinema, sports, foreign travel; KdF Wagon (VW Beetle) promised to workers for 5 marks/week — none ever delivered, factories used for armaments.
p3: SdA (Beauty of Labour): improved workplace facilities like toilets and canteens — but workers had to do the building themselves with no extra pay.

front: What were Nazi beliefs about race?
p1: Eugenics: belief that humans should be selectively bred to produce the 'ideal' Aryan human — forced evolution.
p2: Racial Hygiene: belief in the superiority of the Aryan race; races should be kept separate.
p3: Anti-Semitism: long-established racist beliefs against Jews given legal force under the Nazis. Nazis believed Jewish politicians were behind Dolschstoss (incorrectly).

front: How did Jewish persecution increase before Kristallnacht?
p1: 1933: Jews banned from civil service and teaching; SA boycott of Jewish shops — Star of David and 'Jude' painted on businesses.
p2: 1935: Nuremberg Laws — stripped Jews of German citizenship; banned from marrying non-Jews; required to wear yellow star.
p3: Jews also banned from inheriting land, serving in the army, and many professions; Nazi propaganda portrayed Jews as subhuman.

front: What happened on Kristallnacht?
p1: 9–10 November 1938: triggered by assassination of a German official in Paris by a Polish Jew — used as pretext for organised violence.
p2: Thousands of synagogues and Jewish businesses burned; over 100 Jews killed; 30,000 arrested and sent to concentration camps.
p3: SA, SS and ordinary Germans participated; Jews then fined 1 billion marks for 'the damage' — arrested when they couldn't pay.

front: How were other groups (non-Jews) persecuted by the Nazis?
p1: Slavs taught as inferior race ('Untermenschen'); Roma people ('Gypsies') arrested from 1933, deprived of citizenship 1938, deported 1939.
p2: Homosexuals: 1935 — 4,000 imprisoned; voluntary castration encouraged.
p3: Disabled people: 1933 — all disabled people sterilised; 1939 — T4 euthanasia programme begins.

front: How were communism and capitalism different?
p1: Communism: the state owns all property and industry to ensure a fair share for every citizen; based on writings of Karl Marx.
p2: Capitalism: individuals are free to own property and businesses; competition in markets drives success.
p3: USSR communist since 1917 revolution; USA had experienced anti-communist 'Red Scares' in the 1920s and 1930s.

front: What was the Grand Alliance and the Tehran Conference?
p1: From 1941 USSR, USA and UK united against Nazism — but the alliance had tensions from the start.
p2: Churchill feared world communism; Stalin resented UK/US delaying the second front until 1944 — leaving the USSR fighting alone for 4 years.
p3: Tehran 1943: focused on wartime strategy; vague agreement that Germany would remain weak after the war.

front: What was agreed at the Yalta Conference?
p1: February 1945 (Roosevelt, Stalin, Churchill): Germany to be split into 4 occupation zones; Berlin also split; Germany to pay $20 billion reparations, half to USSR.
p2: Stalin promised Eastern Europe would hold free elections.
p3: Eastern Europe agreed as a Soviet 'sphere of influence' — though the exact meaning was left undefined.

front: What disagreements were there at Yalta?
p1: Poland: Stalin wanted a 'friendly' Polish government; Britain had gone to war to defend Polish independence and refused to give in.
p2: Reparations level disputed — Britain and America feared repeating the mistakes of Versailles.
p3: Definition of the Soviet 'sphere of influence' left dangerously vague — storing up future conflict.

front: Why was there more tension at the Potsdam Conference?
p1: July–August 1945 (Truman, Stalin, Attlee): Hitler's death removed the common enemy; Roosevelt's death replaced a cooperative president with the far more hostile Truman.
p2: Between Yalta and Potsdam, Stalin had installed a communist puppet government in Poland — breaking his Yalta promise.
p3: USA's successful atomic bomb test increased tension; Truman strongly objected to Soviet presence in Eastern Europe and lack of free elections.

front: What was the impact of the first atomic bomb?
p1: 6 and 9 August 1945: atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing hundreds of thousands.
p2: Ushered in the nuclear age — a direct threat to the USSR, which could not yet compete.
p3: Stalin felt threatened that Truman had used the bomb without telling him; deepened mutual suspicion.

front: How did Stalin create Satellite States?
p1: USSR had liberated Eastern Europe from Nazi rule; Stalin turned these states into a 'buffer zone' to protect the USSR from future invasion.
p2: Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia absorbed into the USSR. Hungary, Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia and Albania became communist one-party states 1945–48.
p3: Yugoslavia resisted Stalin and maintained independence under Tito. Churchill declared an 'Iron Curtain' had descended over Europe in 1946.

front: What did the Long and Novikov Telegrams say?
p1: February 1946: George Kennan (US ambassador in Moscow) sent the 8,000-word Long Telegram — Stalin planned destruction of capitalism and world communism, but would back down under pressure.
p2: September 1946: Novikov Telegram — Soviet ambassador reported USA was planning to use military might to dominate the world; cooperation impossible since Roosevelt's death.
p3: Both telegrams hardened attitudes on each side and shaped Cold War strategy.

front: What was the Truman Doctrine?
p1: 1947: Truman declared capitalism as the system of freedom and democracy; communism as repression and violence — a choice between good and evil.
p2: Pledged America would contain communism from spreading further — beginning with a $400 million aid package to Greece and Turkey.
p3: Triggered by Britain's inability to keep financing anti-communist fighters in Greece — USA accepted responsibility to halt the spread of communism.

front: What was the Marshall Plan?
p1: General Marshall toured Europe and saw widespread devastation; convinced Truman to launch $13 billion of aid — Britain and France received largest shares.
p2: Offered to USSR and satellite states but Stalin rejected it, calling it 'Dollar Imperialism'.
p3: British foreign secretary called it 'a lifeline to sinking men'; Europe now divided into two economic camps.

front: What was COMINFORM and COMECON?
p1: COMINFORM (1947): Communist Information Bureau — coordinated policies of communist parties across Soviet satellite states, increasing Soviet control.
p2: COMECON (1949): Council for Mutual Economic Assistance — Soviet equivalent of the Marshall Plan, binding satellite economies to the USSR.
p3: Both were Stalin's response to the Marshall Plan — Europe was now divided into two distinct economic and political blocs.

front: Why did Stalin blockade Berlin?
p1: Stalin feared the West was rebuilding their German zones to create a powerful Germany capable of invading the USSR again.
p2: 1947: US and UK merged zones into 'Bizonia'; March 1948 France joined to make 'Trizonia'; June 1948 the Deutschmark introduced without consulting Stalin.
p3: 24 June 1948: Stalin closed all road and rail links from West Germany to West Berlin — attempting to starve the West out.

front: What was the impact of the Berlin Airlift?
p1: June 1948–May 1949: Western allies airlifted 4,000 tonnes of food and fuel daily into West Berlin. Stalin could not shoot down the planes without risking nuclear war.
p2: Huge propaganda victory for the West — demonstrated capitalism's commitment to its people.
p3: Cemented division of Germany (FRG and GDR established 1949); led to NATO (1949) and Warsaw Pact (1955); USSR developed own nuclear bomb 1949.

front: What were NATO and the Warsaw Pact?
p1: NATO (1949): USA, Britain, France and 9 others — if any member attacked, all would retaliate; led to US military bases across Europe.
p2: West Germany joined NATO 1955 — seen as confirmation the West was creating a dangerous armed Germany.
p3: Warsaw Pact (1955): Soviet equivalent with USSR and satellite states; commanded by Soviet Union — increased confrontation and risk of conflict.

front: How did the arms race develop 1945–60?
p1: 1945: USA develops A-bomb. 1949: USSR develops A-bomb. 1952: USA develops H-bomb (1,000× more powerful than Hiroshima). 1953: USSR develops H-bomb.
p2: 1957: USA develops ICBM (fires nuclear bomb 4,500km). USSR develops it months later.
p3: Led to Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) — neither side could use nuclear weapons without being destroyed in retaliation.

front: What was the space race?
p1: 1957: USSR launched Sputnik — first satellite. Seen as a military threat; USSR also sent dog Laika into space on Sputnik 2.
p2: 1961: USSR sent Yuri Gagarin into orbit — first man in space.
p3: Space race was a propaganda competition as well as a military one — showing whose system was more technologically advanced.

front: What was De-Stalinisation?
p1: 1953: Stalin died; two-year power struggle resulted in Nikita Khrushchev becoming leader in 1955.
p2: Khrushchev's De-Stalinisation policy: condemned Stalin's purges and cult of personality; raised hopes of a more liberal USSR.
p3: Led to cautious optimism in the West about improved relations — but Soviet control of satellite states remained firm.

front: Why were Hungarians protesting in 1956?
p1: Hungary's economy controlled by COMECON — prevented Marshall Aid or free trade with the West; forced to trade on uneven terms with USSR.
p2: Mátyás Rákosi was a brutal dictator who used the AVH secret police to maintain control — killed 2,000 people.
p3: Khrushchev's De-Stalinisation speech (February 1956) raised hopes of reform; food shortages and protests began.

front: What happened during the Hungarian Uprising?
p1: Imre Nagy replaced Rákosi; introduced reforms — ended one-party state, released political prisoners, asked Khrushchev to remove Soviet troops. Khrushchev initially agreed.
p2: Nagy went too far: announced Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact. Khrushchev ordered invasion — 1,000 tanks rolled into Budapest; 3,000 Hungarians killed, 20,000 fled.
p3: Nagy executed 1958; replaced by hard-line communist Kádár. West failed to help — showed America would not intervene in the Soviet sphere.

front: Why did Khrushchev make his Berlin Ultimatum?
p1: During the 1950s over 4 million East Germans (1/5 of the population) fled to the West through the Berlin loophole — many highly skilled, damaging the Eastern economy.
p2: West Germany joined NATO in 1955 — confirming Soviet fears of a rearmed, threatening Germany.
p3: 1958 Berlin Ultimatum: Western allies given 6 months to leave Berlin and declare it a 'free city', or Khrushchev would hand control of transport links to East Germany.

front: Why did the summits of 1959–61 fail to solve the Berlin Crisis?
p1: Geneva (May 1959) and Camp David (September 1959): little achieved, though Khrushchev postponed the six-month deadline.
p2: Paris Summit (1960): collapsed when Khrushchev demanded Eisenhower apologise for the U2 spy plane shot down over the USSR; Eisenhower refused; Khrushchev walked out.
p3: Vienna Summit (1961): Khrushchev saw Kennedy as young and inexperienced; bullied him by reissuing the ultimatum; Kennedy responded by increasing US military spending by $3 billion.

front: What was the Berlin Wall?
p1: Refugee crisis intensified as East Germans feared the border would close — fled in their thousands. East German leader Ulbricht pleaded with Khrushchev to act.
p2: 13 August 1961: barbed wire fence constructed overnight around West Berlin; later fortified into the Berlin Wall.
p3: German families and friends separated overnight — not reunited for 28 years; those attempting to cross were shot, like 18-year-old Peter Fechter.

front: What were the consequences of building the Berlin Wall?
p1: Khrushchev: refugee crisis halted; East economy could recover; communism survived in Berlin; Western spies could no longer easily cross.
p2: Kennedy: Khrushchev had conceded West Berlin would remain capitalist; the Wall became a symbol of Soviet oppression — 'locking people in'.
p3: October 1961: US and Soviet tanks faced off at Checkpoint Charlie for hours — highest tension since the Korean War. JFK exploited the Wall in his 1963 'Ich bin ein Berliner' speech.

front: What was the impact of the Cuban Revolution?
p1: New Year's Day 1959: Fidel Castro and Che Guevara overthrew the US-backed dictator Batista.
p2: Castro nationalised American land and companies; USA boycotted Cuban sugar; Castro turned to Khrushchev, who agreed to buy Cuban sugar.
p3: Cuba — in America's sphere of influence — became communist; seen as a direct threat to US security.

front: What was the Bay of Pigs invasion?
p1: 1961: Kennedy authorised the CIA to train 1,400 Cuban exiles to invade Cuba and overthrow Castro.
p2: The invasion was a disaster — poorly planned and easily defeated; humiliated America and revealed US hypocrisy.
p3: Castro realised his vulnerability and sought further Soviet support; Khrushchev began installing nuclear missiles in Cuba.

front: How did America react to discovery of Soviet missiles in Cuba?
p1: 14 October 1962: Soviet missiles in Cuba spotted by a U2 spyplane. Kennedy convened ExComm to review options.
p2: Options considered: military attack (risks MAD); diplomacy (seen as weak after Berlin); naval blockade chosen.
p3: Kennedy announced that any Soviet ship crossing the blockade would be fired upon — 13 days of crisis followed.

front: What happened during the 13 days of crisis (1962)?
p1: Soviet ships sailed towards the blockade; the world held its breath. Letters exchanged between Kennedy and Khrushchev seeking a solution.
p2: 24 October: Soviet ships reached the blockade, stopped, and turned around — Khrushchev 'blinked'.
p3: 27 October: U2 spyplane shot down over Cuba; Kennedy's advisors urged retaliation — Kennedy refused. Crisis resolved 28 October.

front: How was the Cuban Missile Crisis resolved?
p1: 28 October 1962: America agreed to secretly remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey and not invade Cuba.
p2: In return, Soviet missiles were publicly removed from Cuba.
p3: Kennedy seen as having 'won' — Khrushchev backed down publicly; secret Turkey deal allowed both to save face.

front: What were the consequences of the Cuban Missile Crisis?
p1: Khrushchev humiliated — ousted in 1964 and replaced by Brezhnev.
p2: 1963: nuclear hotline (direct phone line) established between Washington and Moscow; Limited Test Ban Treaty — no more above-ground nuclear testing.
p3: 1968: Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty — no sharing of nuclear weapons with other countries.

front: What was the Prague Spring?
p1: January 1968: Alexander Dubček became new communist leader of Czechoslovakia — called for 'Socialism with a Human Face'.
p2: Introduced: free speech, abolished censorship, curbed secret police, increased trade with West, announced 10-year programme for democratic elections.
p3: Background: Czechoslovakia had been a democracy before WWII; Stalinist Novotný's rule was deeply unpopular; economy run for benefit of USSR not Czechoslovakia.

front: Why did the USSR invade Czechoslovakia?
p1: Brezhnev feared Czechoslovakia was becoming too capitalist and Soviet control would weaken.
p2: Feared Czechoslovakia would leave the Warsaw Pact — Marshal Tito's visit to Prague in summer 1968 intensified this fear.
p3: Hard-line Warsaw Pact leaders Ulbricht (East Germany) and Gomulka (Poland) begged Brezhnev to intervene — feared the reforms spreading to their countries.

front: What happened during the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia?
p1: August 1968: USSR, Poland, Hungary, Bulgaria and East Germany invaded with 500,000 troops.
p2: Dubček captured by Soviet paratroopers, taken to Moscow and forced to abandon his reforms; replaced by hard-line Gustáv Husák.
p3: 150 Czechoslovak civilians killed; Jan Palach set himself on fire in protest; Albania left Warsaw Pact in protest.

front: What was the Brezhnev Doctrine?
p1: Issued by Brezhnev to justify the invasion of Czechoslovakia: if any communist country showed signs of turning towards capitalism, all communist countries had a duty to force it back.
p2: Formalised the Soviet right to invade any satellite state that threatened the communist bloc.
p3: Later replaced by Gorbachev's 'Sinatra Doctrine' in 1988 — allowing satellite states to 'go their own way'.

front: How did other countries respond to the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia?
p1: America failed to help — too busy with Vietnam; confirmed again that the West would not intervene in the Soviet sphere.
p2: Albania left the Warsaw Pact in protest; Yugoslavia and Romania condemned the invasion and began fostering closer links with China.
p3: Western communist parties cut ties with the USSR in protest — weakened Soviet ideological influence in Western Europe.

front: Why did the USA want détente in the 1970s?
p1: Late 1960s: huge social and racial tensions in American cities following Martin Luther King's assassination in 1968 — money needed for domestic issues.
p2: USA had been fighting (and losing) the Vietnam War against communist North Vietnam since 1965, spending billions per year.
p3: Hoped improved relations with USSR would help persuade North Vietnam to agree a ceasefire; also sought to open communist markets for American goods.

front: Why did the USSR want détente in the 1970s?
p1: USSR spending roughly 40% of all income on nuclear weaponry — economically unsustainable.
p2: Keen to gain access to American technology and grain as the Soviet economy was much poorer than the West.
p3: Cuban Missile Crisis had revealed how close both sides came to nuclear war — motivated arms reduction talks.

front: What was SALT 1?
p1: 1972: Strategic Arms Limitation Talks — Nixon and Brezhnev signed SALT I.
p2: Interim Treaty: restrictions on numbers of ICBMs and SLBMs; Anti-Ballistic Missiles limited to 2 sites each.
p3: Both sides still had enough nuclear weapons for MAD — but it symbolised improving relations; Nixon and Brezhnev visited each other in 1972/3.

front: What were the Helsinki Accords? (1975)
p1: 33 nations from NATO and Warsaw Pact met in Helsinki; agreed 3 'baskets': Basket 1 — European borders inviolable; Basket 2 — economic and scientific cooperation; Basket 3 — human rights to be respected.
p2: Followed by Apollo-Soyuz Mission — US and Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit, symbolising the spirit of détente.
p3: Seen as the zenith of détente but in practice 'just a piece of paper' — human rights basket largely ignored by USSR.

front: Was Détente successful?
p1: SALT I and Helsinki Accords reduced direct military tension and opened dialogue between superpowers.
p2: SALT II proposed greater bans on bombers and ICBMs — but stalled and cancelled by Carter due to growing distrust and the Iranian hostage crisis 1979.
p3: Collapsed entirely with Soviet invasion of Afghanistan 1979 — détente ended; Second Cold War began.

front: Why did the Mujahedeen emerge in Afghanistan?
p1: 1978: communist PDPA seized power in Afghanistan.
p2: Many Afghans rejected the communist government — its atheism directly conflicted with their Muslim faith.
p3: Communists imprisoned, tortured and murdered Muslim religious leaders — triggering the formation of the anti-communist Mujahedeen resistance movement.

front: Why did the USSR invade Afghanistan?
p1: Mujahedeen were overpowering the communist Afghan government; Brezhnev feared this would inspire rebellion in the USSR's own Muslim regions.
p2: Christmas Day 1979: USSR invaded to prop up the communist government.
p3: Soviets killed the unpopular President Amin and replaced him with the more pro-Moscow but still unpopular Kamal.

front: What happened during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan?
p1: 10-year war costing the USSR $8 billion per year; estimated 15,000 Soviet soldiers killed.
p2: Red Army ill-prepared for Afghan landscape; Mujahedeen fought an effective guerrilla war.
p3: War deeply unpopular at home in the USSR — compared by critics to America's Vietnam.

front: What was the impact of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan?
p1: Carter alarmed by Soviet presence near the Persian Gulf (US oil interests); issued Carter Doctrine — America would respond strongly to any attempt to control the Persian Gulf.
p2: Economic sanctions on USSR — end of grain trade; America supplied weapons to the Mujahedeen.
p3: Olympic boycotts: USA refused 1980 Moscow Olympics; USSR refused 1984 Los Angeles Olympics. SALT II cancelled — détente officially dead.

front: How did Reagan increase Cold War tensions?
p1: Reagan called USSR an 'Evil Empire', 'focus of evil in the modern world', compared them to the Nazis.
p2: Reagan Doctrine: USA would fund and support anti-communist resistance groups worldwide (e.g. Nicaragua); invaded Grenada to topple communist regime 1983.
p3: Raised military spending by $1 trillion.

front: What was Reagan's SDI?
p1: 1983: Strategic Defence Initiative ('Star Wars') — announced orbital laser system to shoot down Soviet missiles and undermine MAD.
p2: Terrified the USSR as they were in no financial position to compete — directly led to Gorbachev's rise and New Thinking.
p3: Was actually a bluff — only in development; Reagan announced it as if it was ready.

front: Why did Gorbachev introduce New Thinking?
p1: Brezhnev's 'era of stagnation': Soviet economy failing; 40% of income spent on nuclear weapons; $8 billion/year on Afghanistan war with no results.
p2: 1986 Chernobyl nuclear meltdown cost $18 billion to contain; poor living standards causing unrest in satellite states (e.g. Poland 1981).
p3: Gorbachev became leader 1985 — concluded radical reform was essential to save the USSR.

front: What was Perestroika and Glasnost?
p1: Perestroika ('Restructuring'): individuals and foreigners could now invest in businesses; Soviet state retained control of key industries.
p2: Glasnost ('Openness'): greater freedom of speech and press; political prisoners released; citizens encouraged to discuss solutions to Soviet problems.
p3: 1988: Sinatra Doctrine replaced the Brezhnev Doctrine — satellite states free to 'go their own way'; aimed to ease military spending but severely undermined Soviet control in Europe.

front: What was the INF Treaty?
p1: Washington 1987: Intermediate Range Nuclear Force Treaty signed by Reagan and Gorbachev.
p2: Agreed to destroy all intermediate-range nuclear missiles — a major, verifiable arms reduction.
p3: Showed Reagan felt he could work with Gorbachev — a qualitative shift from the early 1980s confrontation.

front: What happened in Eastern Europe in 1989?
p1: Gorbachev's New Thinking sparked unrest — citizens saw freedoms in the USSR and demanded the same; hard-line leaders like Honecker (East Germany) refused to reform.
p2: June 1989: Poland first to abandon communism — Solidarity won elections; when Gorbachev sent no tanks, other states followed rapidly.
p3: Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria, Romania all abandoned communism by end of 1989; Romania involved violent revolution. All Eastern Europe capitalist within 6 months.

front: What was the impact of the fall of the Berlin Wall?
p1: 9 November 1989: crowds gathered at the Wall; East German guards stood down; people tore it down.
p2: German families and friends reunited after 28 years of separation.
p3: Germany officially reunified October 1990; Warsaw Pact dissolved July 1991 — symbolised the end of the Cold War.

front: How did Gorbachev lose control over the USSR?
p1: Gorbachev seen as a hero in the West (Nobel Peace Prize 1990) but regarded as weak in the USSR.
p2: Soviet republics saw how easily satellite states had gained independence and demanded the same — 1990: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania declared independence.
p3: Boris Yeltsin, president of Russia (the largest republic), began openly defying Gorbachev in early 1991.

front: What happened during the August Coup?
p1: August 1991: 8 hard-line communist leaders staged a coup, removing Gorbachev from power and abolishing Glasnost and Perestroika.
p2: Boris Yeltsin led the resistance and overthrew the coup after just 3 days, restoring Gorbachev — but the affair exposed how little power Gorbachev had left.
p3: Christmas Day 1991: Gorbachev resigned and announced the breakup of the USSR to avoid civil war; Yeltsin became 1st president of capitalist Russia.

front: What was society like in Elizabethan England?
p1: Majority rural; high levels of poverty. Society was hierarchical — everyone expected to keep their place.
p2: Nobles (dukes/earls): most powerful below Elizabeth; owned huge land, could raise armies. Gentry: less wealthy landowners, often JPs. Merchants: wealthy town traders represented in parliament.
p3: Peasants: vast majority; entirely powerless.

front: What was the role of Parliament and the Privy Council?
p1: Privy Council: 19 key advisors including William Cecil, Robert Dudley and Francis Walsingham.
p2: Parliament: needed to approve taxation; Elizabeth reluctant to call it too often.
p3: Royal prerogative: Elizabeth alone decided foreign policy, religion, succession and marriage.

front: What are key differences between Protestantism and Catholicism?
p1: Catholics: Pope is head of the Church; services in Latin; seven sacraments; priests cannot marry.
p2: Protestants: monarch is head of the Church; services in English; Bible is the sole authority; only two sacraments (baptism and communion).
p3: England had oscillated between Protestant (Edward VI) and Catholic (Mary I) before Elizabeth — leaving the country deeply divided.

front: What was controversial about the marriage of Henry VIII and Elizabeth's mother?
p1: Henry VIII divorced Catherine of Aragon to marry Anne Boleyn (Elizabeth's mother) — the Pope had not sanctioned the divorce.
p2: Catholics therefore regarded the marriage as invalid and Elizabeth as illegitimate and unfit to be queen.
p3: Henry VIII himself declared Elizabeth illegitimate in the 2nd Act of Succession 1536 — though he reversed this in the 3rd Act 1543.

front: Why did some people view Elizabeth I as illegitimate?
p1: Catholics argued Henry VIII's marriage to Anne Boleyn was invalid as the Pope had not approved his divorce from Catherine of Aragon.
p2: This made Elizabeth illegitimate in Catholic eyes — and therefore the wrong person to be queen.
p3: The Catholic alternative claimant was Mary, Queen of Scots — strengthening the legitimacy threat.

front: What were beliefs about female power in the 16th century?
p1: Elizabethan England was highly patriarchal — it was widely believed women could not control men in government or lead an army.
p2: The only previous queen regnant was her half-sister 'Bloody Mary' — whose reign left the impression that female rulers were unstable.
p3: It was expected Elizabeth would marry; a Tudor wife was legally required to obey her husband — unacceptable for a monarch.

front: What were relations between England and foreign powers like in 1558?
p1: Spain: most powerful country in the world under Philip II (former husband of Mary I, had proposed to Elizabeth); controlled the New World and the Netherlands.
p2: France: 2nd most powerful; England's traditional enemy; at war with England at the start of the reign until the 1559 Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis (Elizabeth gave up Calais).
p3: Scotland: independent, ruled by Mary, Queen of Scots (in France married to Prince Francis); bound to France by the Auld Alliance.

front: What was the impact of the French war at the start of Elizabeth's reign?
p1: England at war with France when Elizabeth took the throne — she had inherited a debt of £227,000 from Mary I.
p2: 1559 Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis: Elizabeth relinquished England's claim to Calais — a humiliation but ended the costly war.
p3: Forced Elizabeth to sell off crown lands to raise quick income — reducing future rental revenues.

front: What were the religious divides in England in 1558?
p1: Henry VIII's break with Rome in 1534 began 25 years of religious turmoil — Protestant under Edward VI, Catholic under Mary I.
p2: Mary I burned c.300 Protestants at the stake; over 800 extreme Protestants fled to Europe.
p3: Elizabeth inherited Catholic bishops and clergy from Mary; majority of the population — especially in the North and West — were likely Catholic; Elizabeth herself was Protestant.

front: What was the Religious Settlement?
p1: Act of Supremacy: Elizabeth declared 'supreme governor' of the Church of England; all clergy and officials had to swear loyalty.
p2: Act of Uniformity: all churches had to use the English Book of Common Prayer; everyone had to attend a licensed church on Sundays (fined 1 shilling as a recusant if not).
p3: Royal Injunctions: Catholic pilgrimages and saints denounced; images and vestments allowed; all churches to hold an English Bible.

front: What was the role of the Church of England in society?
p1: Church attendance was compulsory — the Church reached into every community in England through its parish structure.
p2: Parish priests were key communicators of royal policy — sermons spread government messages.
p3: Visitations enforced the Act of Uniformity — inspectors checked churches were following the settlement correctly.

front: Why did Puritans dislike the Religious Settlement?
p1: Objected to Catholic elements retained in the settlement: images, vestments, church hierarchy.
p2: Disliked the vague wording of the Book of Common Prayer — it left too much room for Catholic interpretation of communion.
p3: Wanted a more thoroughly Protestant settlement — direct line to God without priestly hierarchy.

front: Were the Puritans a serious threat?
p1: Threat: had support from key Privy Council members (Leicester, Walsingham); some became bishops to alter the settlement; persistent Puritan MPs Strickland and Cope pressed for change in Parliament.
p2: In the Crucifix Controversy they forced Elizabeth to back down — crucifixes removed from all churches except her personal chapel.
p3: Not a threat: no foreign support or alternative monarch; tiny minority (a few thousand); divided with no clear leader; several Puritan MPs imprisoned for challenging the settlement.

front: Why did Catholics not rebel before 1568?
p1: Settlement was more acceptable than feared — Elizabeth's tolerance kept the peace; recusancy fines of 1 shilling were not devastating.
p2: Pope did not excommunicate Elizabeth until 1570 — 11 years for Catholics to adjust to the settlement.
p3: France and Spain were too distracted by their own problems (Dutch Revolt, French Wars of Religion) to support Catholic rebellion.

front: Why was Mary, Queen of Scots a threat to Elizabeth 1558–68?
p1: Catholics viewed Mary as the true Queen of England — Elizabeth's illegitimacy in Catholic eyes made Mary the rightful heir.
p2: Mary's marriage to Lord Darnley strengthened her claim — both had claims to the English throne; their son James (b.1566) highlighted Elizabeth's lack of an heir.
p3: 1560: Scottish protestant lords signed the Treaty of Edinburgh giving up Mary's claim to the English throne — Mary never accepted it.

front: Why did Mary, Queen of Scots come to England and what was the York Conference?
p1: 1567: Mary deposed by Scottish Protestant lords — suspected of involvement in assassination of her 2nd husband Lord Darnley.
p2: 1568: Mary escaped imprisonment, fled to England seeking Elizabeth's aid — leaving Elizabeth with an impossible dilemma: help, hand over, imprison, or allow her to flee to the continent.
p3: Following the York Conference, Elizabeth chose imprisonment — keeping Mary as a pawn but preventing her from becoming a rallying point for Catholic invasion.

front: Why did the Northern Earls rebel?
p1: Religion: Earls of Westmoreland and Northumberland wanted to restore Catholicism to England.
p2: Politics: as Catholics, the earls had lost centuries of power in the North, replaced by Protestants — hoped Mary, Queen of Scots on the throne would restore their position.
p3: No clear foreign support and most other Catholic nobles refused to join — the rebellion was poorly supported from the start.

front: Why did the Revolt of the Northern Earls fail?
p1: Earls called on Catholic nobles to join — none came. Captured Hartlepool hoping for Spanish aid — none arrived.
p2: Mary, Queen of Scots moved south to Coventry — removed from the earls' reach.
p3: Elizabeth's army of 14,000 faced them; the earls fled to Scotland. 450 rebels executed; Northumberland's head displayed at York.

front: How serious was Papal Excommunication?
p1: 1570: Pope Pius V excommunicated Elizabeth and released all Catholics from loyalty to her — theoretically making it a Catholic's duty to overthrow her.
p2: 1571: Elizabeth made it treason to possess or spread copies of the Papal Bull.
p3: In practice, the excommunication increased the Catholic threat by giving foreign powers religious justification to invade — but France and Spain were still too preoccupied to act.

front: How did Walsingham's spies keep Elizabeth safe?
p1: Francis Walsingham built an extensive network of spies across Europe — intercepted letters and infiltrated Catholic plots.
p2: Discovered the Ridolfi Plot (1571), Throckmorton Plot (1583) and Babington Plot (1586) before they could succeed.
p3: In the Babington Plot, Walsingham deliberately let the plot run to obtain written evidence proving Mary, Queen of Scots' direct involvement.

front: What happened in the Ridolfi and Throckmorton Plots?
p1: Ridolfi Plot (1571): Pope's spy Ridolfi planned the Duke of Norfolk to lead a rebellion with Spanish support to make Mary queen; discovered by Cecil — Norfolk executed.
p2: Throckmorton Plot (1583): French Catholic army to invade, free Mary, start a Catholic rebellion backed by Philip of Spain; discovered by Walsingham; plotters tortured and executed.
p3: Both plots led Cecil and Walsingham to agree the Bond of Association (1584): both swore to execute anyone found to be plotting against Elizabeth.

front: What happened in the Babington Plot?
p1: 1586: French and Spanish forces planned to invade England and free Mary. Walsingham discovered the plot early but let it continue.
p2: Walsingham intercepted letters until he found one from Mary directly encouraging the plot — conclusive proof of treason.
p3: Mary tried by parliament, found guilty of treason.

front: What led to Mary, Queen of Scots' execution?
p1: Despite proof of involvement in the Babington Plot, Elizabeth was reluctant to execute a cousin and an anointed monarch — feared setting a precedent that parliaments could execute monarchs.
p2: Cecil and Walsingham knew the Spanish Armada was imminent — Mary as a Spanish pawn had to be removed.
p3: Elizabeth signed the death warrant but forbade its use; Privy Council ignored her and Cecil sent it in secret. February 1587: Mary executed at Fotheringhay Castle.

front: Why did England and Spain become rivals?
p1: Religious rivalry: Philip II wanted England Catholic again; 1570 Papal excommunication made it a Catholic duty to overthrow Elizabeth; 1584 Treaty of Joinville — France and Spain pledged to destroy Protestantism.
p2: Commercial rivalry: English cloth trade collapse in 1550s forced merchants to seek new markets; Spanish controlled the most valuable New World trade routes.
p3: Drake raided Spanish ports and treasure ships with Elizabeth's secret backing — £40,000 from Panama 1572; £400,000 during circumnavigation 1577–80. Elizabeth's knighting of Drake in 1580 inflamed Spain.

front: What was England's involvement in the Dutch Revolt?
p1: From 1566 Protestant Dutch revolted against Catholic Spanish rule; Elizabeth supplied weapons and money secretly — eager to keep Spain distracted.
p2: 1584: Dutch leader William of Orange assassinated — revolt in danger of collapse; Elizabeth signed Treaty of Nonsuch (1585) committing 7,400 troops and £126,000/year.
p3: England and Spain were now formally at war.

front: What did Dudley do in the Netherlands?
p1: Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, sent with an army after the Treaty of Nonsuch — but lacked enough men, money or supplies to defeat Parma's superior force.
p2: Only managed to slow Parma's progress; faced betrayals from commanders.
p3: Key success: prevented Parma capturing the deep-water port of Ostend — stopping Parma's troops boarding the Armada quickly.

front: What did Drake do at Cadiz?
p1: 1587: Walsingham's spies reported a great Armada being built at Cadiz. Drake sent to buy England time.
p2: Drake slipped into Cadiz harbour on a moonless night with four ships; destroyed 30 Spanish ships and damaged more; raided precious food and supply barrels.
p3: Drake then raided Portugal and captured a Spanish treasure ship worth £140,000 — brought England 12 months to prepare for the Armada.

front: What was Philip II's plan for the Armada?
p1: Duke of Medina-Sidonia to sail 130 ships and 27,000 men to the Spanish Netherlands.
p2: Rendezvous with Duke of Parma and his 30,000 men; combined force to invade England and kill Elizabeth.
p3: Plan fatally dependent on Parma and the Armada meeting at exactly the right time — Parma was 6 days' march from Calais when the Armada arrived.

front: How did English tactics defeat the Armada?
p1: Drake's raid on Cadiz gained England 12 months to prepare — warning beacons built along the coast; faster galleons constructed.
p2: English navy (Drake and Lord Howard) chased the slow Armada up the Channel, harrying from long range — Spanish could not board in the open sea.
p3: Fireships sent into the anchored Armada at Calais — Spanish fleet scattered and broke formation; decisive English attack at the Battle of Gravelines (6 August 1588).

front: How did Spanish poor planning defeat the Armada?
p1: Armada led by inexperienced Medina-Sidonia — first-choice commander Santa Cruz had died.
p2: Miscommunication: Parma not in Calais on time; failure to capture deep-water port of Ostend meant boarding Parma's troops would have taken 3 days even with perfect communication.
p3: Drake's Cadiz raid meant Spain had insufficient food and supply barrels — many Spanish soldiers starved.

front: How did wind and weather defeat the Armada?
p1: After Gravelines, wind blew the Armada north around Scotland and Ireland — unfamiliar, rough seas.
p2: 40 ships shipwrecked in storms; fewer than 80 ships and fewer than 10,000 men returned to Spain.
p3: English galleons were faster and more manoeuvrable than Spanish transport ships — though only 24 of the English fleet were galleons.

front: How did the defeat of the Armada boost Elizabeth?
p1: At Tilbury during the Armada, Elizabeth addressed her army in full armour aged 55: 'I have the heart and stomach of a king' — challenged gender expectations.
p2: Victory suggested God was on the Protestants' side — commemorative medal issued: 'God blew, and they were scattered'.
p3: Defeat of the most powerful nation in the world boosted English confidence; more confidence to explore, trade and attack Spain. Armada bankrupted Philip.

front: What was education like in Elizabeth's reign?
p1: By end of reign 30% of men and 10% of women were literate (up from 20% and 10% at the start). 72 new Grammar Schools established.
p2: Nobility: sons learned Latin, Greek, history, philosophy, government, theology. Girls also educated — Elizabeth herself was highly educated.
p3: Working class: education not available; children worked from early age. Some poor boys of promise attended grammar schools funded by wealthy donors.

front: What were the leisure activities of the poor?
p1: Football: often led to deaths — no rules. Gambling on bear-baiting (chained bear fighting dogs) and cock-fighting.
p2: Hunting rabbit. Music heard at fairs, markets, pubs and church.
p3: Theatre: 1 penny to stand in the 'pit' — close to the action, noisy and popular with all classes.

front: What were the leisure activities of the rich?
p1: Hunting on horseback (male and female), hawking, fishing, fencing, real tennis, wrestling.
p2: Luxury goods like tobacco from the New World; employed household musicians.
p3: Theatre: wealthy paid for seats in the galleries. Literature and poetry — patronage of writers like Shakespeare.

front: What was the Elizabethan Theatre like?
p1: Protestantism encouraged secular (non-religious) plays — replaced medieval Bible stories. Theatres backed by powerful nobles like the Earl of Leicester.
p2: 1576: The Theatre opened; followed by the Rose (1586) and the Globe (1599). Open to all social classes — 1 penny for the pit.
p3: From 1572 all plays had to be approved by the Queen's official — some censorship. Puritans opposed theatre as sinful and satanic.

front: How did population rise lead to poverty?
p1: Population grew by around 1/3 in Elizabeth's reign — greater demand for land meant landlords raised rents.
p2: More people meant greater demand for food — rising food prices. Also greater supply of labour — employers could pay less.
p3: Combined effect of rising prices and falling wages created widespread poverty, especially in the countryside.

front: How did enclosure lead to poverty?
p1: Enclosure: wealthy landowners claimed common farmland, hedged it and used it to graze sheep instead of growing crops.
p2: Poor labourers lost their land and income; food prices rose as less was being grown.
p3: Displaced labourers became vagabonds — wandering in search of work and regarded with fear and hostility.

front: How did debasement lead to poverty?
p1: During the 1540s the currency was debased — precious metal removed from coins to create more of them; value of coins fell; prices rose.
p2: Inflation already high from population growth; debasement made it worse.
p3: Dissolution of the monasteries (Henry VIII, 1530s) removed the safety net for the poor — especially in the North.

front: What were Elizabethan attitudes to the poor?
p1: Key distinction: deserving (impotent) poor — old, sick, disabled — deserved help. Undeserving (able-bodied) poor — fit to work but unemployed — treated harshly.
p2: Puritans believed idleness was a sin; feared exaggerated numbers of vagabonds could stir revolts; blamed vagabonds for plague outbreaks.
p3: Vagabonds associated with crime — with little law enforcement, hostility was widespread.

front: How were the poor treated by new laws?
p1: Statute of Artificers (1563): established maximum national wages for specific jobs to deter economic migration.
p2: Vagabonds Act (1572): vagabonds over 14 whipped and burned through the right ear; sent to House of Correction on 2nd offence; JPs had to register the poor and collect a poor rate.
p3: Act for the Relief of the Poor (1576): towns required to find work for the undeserving poor; those refusing work sent to a House of Correction.

front: What new technologies made it easier to explore?
p1: 1569 Mercator Map: new accurate world map made long-distance navigation safer.
p2: Astrolabe: allowed navigators to determine latitude by measuring the angle of the North Star.
p3: English galleons: faster and more manoeuvrable with greater cargo space; low bow and stern increased stability in ocean conditions.

front: Why did Elizabethans explore?
p1: Spanish controlled the most valuable New World trade; English sought to plunder Spanish routes and find new markets after the collapse of the Dutch cloth trade in the 1550s.
p2: Financial gain and fame: Drake returned from circumnavigation with £400,000 of Spanish gold; new luxury goods (tobacco, cocoa, potatoes) could be sold at high prices.
p3: 1561: John Hawkins created the Triangular Slave Trade — beginning large amounts of wealth for England.

front: What happened during Drake's Circumnavigation?
p1: 1577–80: Drake was raiding Spanish colonies in South America; pursued by Spanish ships so escaped into the Pacific — circumnavigation was unplanned.
p2: Returned with over £400,000 of Spanish gold (almost £500 million today); became 2nd person in history and 1st Englishman to circumnavigate the globe.
p3: Established a short-lived colony near San Francisco (Nova Albion); publicly knighted by Elizabeth on the deck of the Golden Hind 1580 — inflaming Spain.

front: What went wrong in the planning of the colony of Virginia?
p1: Poor leadership: Raleigh organised and financed the voyages but never went himself; Ralph Lane led the 1585 colony but lacked the skills to manage relations with Native Americans or sustain the settlement.
p2: All food stored on one ship — The Tiger — making the colony fatally vulnerable when it hit a reef and seawater destroyed the supplies.
p3: Wrong colonists sent: too many merchants, soldiers and craftsmen; almost no one who could farm the land or produce food for a long-term settlement.

front: What happened at Roanoke Island?
p1: 1585 (first colony): The Tiger hit a reef destroying food supplies — colonists immediately dependent on the Algonquian people. Relations deteriorated as Native Americans blamed the English for spreading disease; Lane massacred Wingina's village and decapitated him. Colony abandoned.
p2: 1587 (second colony): John White returned with new settlers but arrived too late to plant crops. Attacked by forces led by Wanchese; White sailed back to England for help — the Spanish Armada prevented his return for three years.
p3: 1590: White returned to find the colony completely abandoned — only the word Croatoan carved into a tree. The 117 colonists were never seen again.

front: What was England like in the Medieval period?
p1: Majority rural society; most people were peasants farming the land with little power or wealth.
p2: England was repeatedly invaded and settled — Vikings from Scandinavia, Normans from France.
p3: Religion dominated life — the Catholic Church was central to government, law and culture.

front: Why did the Vikings come to England?
p1: Economic: Vikings came to trade and later to raid, attracted by England's wealth and weak coastal defences compared to scarce resources in Scandinavia.
p2: Military: 865 — Great Heathen Army invaded seeking revenge for the murder of Ragnar Lodbrok by King Ælla of Northumbria.
p3: Settlement: 878 — Viking conquests led to creation of the Danelaw; Vikings encouraged to settle across North and East England.

front: What was the Viking experience in the Danelaw?
p1: 878: Treaty between Alfred and Guthrum — Vikings allowed to settle in the Danelaw; established towns and farming communities.
p2: 1016: Viking king Cnut conquered all England — promoted acceptance and peace between Vikings and English.
p3: Vikings faced hostility: 1002 — King Æthelred ordered the St Brice's Day Massacre — death of all Danes in England.

front: How did the Vikings impact England?
p1: Trade: Vikings brought trade links from Europe and the Middle East to the Danelaw; York became an international trading hub.
p2: Government: Vikings introduced 'Things' — local democratic assemblies where communities voted on laws and decided guilt (early juries).
p3: Language: Old Norse heavily influenced English — days of the week (e.g. Thursday = Thor's day); many place names ending in -by or -thorpe.

front: Case Study: York under the Vikings
p1: York grew from a town of 1,000 in 850 to a city of around 15,000 people by 950 — one of the largest cities in England.
p2: Became an international trading hub — merchants travelled from across Europe and the Middle East to trade there.
p3: Archaeological evidence at Coppergate shows Norse crafts, jewellery, and goods from as far as Constantinople — a genuinely multicultural city.

front: Why did Normans invade England in 1066?
p1: King Edward the Confessor died without children; William of Normandy claimed Edward had named him as heir.
p2: William promised any Norman knight who supported the invasion land and power in England.
p3: Pope supported the invasion — gave religious legitimacy to William's claim; William carried a Papal banner at the Battle of Hastings.

front: What was life like for the Normans after 1066?
p1: Normans became the ruling class — given land and positions at the top of the Feudal System by William.
p2: Faced rebellions from the English — Normans increased oppression and control (built 84 castles using Jewish loans) to maintain power.
p3: French was the official language of England for 200 years after 1066 — though the poor continued to speak English.

front: How did the Normans impact England?
p1: Feudal System: imposed a strict hierarchy — King, barons, knights, English peasants at the bottom. The Normans formed the ruling class for centuries.
p2: Built environment: hundreds of castles and cathedrals; introduced Norman surnames; Norman French heavily influenced the English language.
p3: Church: brought the English Church into line with Rome; replaced English bishops with Norman ones; built thousands of churches, cathedrals and monasteries.

front: Why did the kings initially protect Jewish moneylenders?
p1: 1070: William I invited Jewish moneylenders to England — Papal ban on usury (charging interest) meant only Jews could legally lend money at interest.
p2: Kings relied on Jewish loans to fund castles, wars and government — 8% of royal income came from Jewish communities.
p3: 1135: Royal Charter granted liberties to Jews; Jewries (Jewish communities) developed across England. 84 castles built using Jewish loans.

front: Why did attitudes to Jews in medieval England change?
p1: 1144: First blood libel stories emerged in Norwich — Jews falsely accused of murdering Christian children for rituals.
p2: 1189: Large-scale anti-Semitic riots across England; 150 Jews committed suicide in York Castle to avoid massacre.
p3: 1265: Pope allowed Christians to perform usury — Jews no longer needed for royal finance; their protected status began to crumble.

front: How did royal treatment of Medieval Jews worsen?
p1: 1100s: English kings steadily increased taxation of Jewish communities.
p2: 1200s: Henry III introduced restrictions — Tabula (yellow badge) enforced; Jewish community increasingly scapegoated.
p3: 1275: Statute of Jewry banned Jews from usury. 1290: Edward I expelled all Jews — over 3,000 forced into exile.

front: What was the impact of Medieval Jewish communities?
p1: Jewish loans funded major building projects including 84 Norman castles and royal government.
p2: 8% of royal income came from Jewish communities — crucial to English state finances.
p3: After expulsion in 1290, Edward I invited Italian banking families to fill the financial gap — showing how dependent the Crown had been on Jewish finance.

front: Why did European traders and craftsmen come to England?
p1: 14th–15th centuries: cloth trade was highly profitable in England — Flemish weavers and Hansa merchants came to profit.
p2: 1351: Edward III invited Flemish weavers to develop the cloth trade after they were evicted from their French hometowns during the Hundred Years' War.
p3: 1303: Edward I gave Hansa merchants permission to establish the Steelyard in London — trading wool and cloth to Northern Europe.

front: What was the experience of European traders and craftsmen?
p1: Normally lived in harmony with English neighbours during prosperous times.
p2: 1381: foreign merchants attacked during the Peasants' Revolt — 150 murdered.
p3: Craft guilds resented migrants as job competition — especially hostile to Flemish weavers; 1440: alien taxes introduced.

front: What was the impact of European traders and craftsmen?
p1: Flemish weavers transformed Colchester — from the 53rd to the 13th richest town in England.
p2: Hansa merchants helped make the wool trade extremely profitable; the Steelyard became a major trading base in London.
p3: European craftsmen introduced new techniques in weaving, metalwork and trade that significantly boosted the English economy.

front: How did England change in the Early Modern period?
p1: Protestant Reformation in the 1500s made England a 'safe haven' for Protestant refugees from Europe.
p2: English involvement in the Transatlantic Slave Trade increased significantly — many enslaved Africans brought to England.
p3: East India Company (1600) began developing trade in India — first Lascars and Ayahs arrived in England.

front: Why did the Huguenots come to England?
p1: Huguenots were French Protestants fleeing Catholic persecution — St Bartholomew's Day Massacre (1572) killed 30,000 Huguenots in France.
p2: First wave: 1560s–70s. Second wave: 1680s — French Catholic monarchy increased persecution; approximately 50,000 settled in London.
p3: England's Protestant identity made it a natural refuge; government actively welcomed skilled Protestant workers.

front: What was the experience of Huguenot migrants?
p1: 1681: Charles II granted all Huguenots Denizen status — legal protection and residency rights.
p2: 1680s: tensions in Spitalfields between Huguenots and English workers who accused them of stealing jobs.
p3: 1600s: many English people donated money to help Huguenots settle — viewed with sympathy as Protestant victims of persecution.

front: What was the impact of Huguenot migrants?
p1: Helped found the Bank of England in 1694; started the English paper industry — 200 paper mills by 1714.
p2: Transformed Spitalfields into a prosperous weaver town; cloth exports were 20 times higher by the end of the 17th century than at its start.
p3: Huguenot scientists contributed to development of inoculations; 2/3 of printers in England were European migrants.

front: Case Study: Huguenots in 17th Century England
p1: Settled in Spitalfields, East London — transformed it into a weaving centre with silk production.
p2: Founded the Bank of England (1694) and started the English paper industry.
p3: By the late 1600s the Huguenot community in London had a positive relationship with the mayor and city authorities.

front: Case Study: Flemish migrants in Sandwich
p1: 1560s: local government of Sandwich invited Flemish weavers to support the local economy following the Dutch Revolt.
p2: Initially seen as positive — introduced new weaving techniques and boosted trade.
p3: Over time: increasing restrictions and hostility as Flemish migrants were accused of 'taking English jobs'; growing tensions by the 1580s.

front: Case Study: Walloon migrants in Canterbury
p1: 1570s: local government of Canterbury invited Walloon migrants (French-speaking Protestants from the Netherlands) to boost the local economy.
p2: Walloons became highly successful — employed English people and taught them their skills; Canterbury became prosperous.
p3: 1580s: Walloons seen as a positive influence in Canterbury — contrast with the more hostile reception in Sandwich.

front: Why did Oliver Cromwell allow Jewish migrants to return to England in 1656?
p1: Jews had been expelled from England since 1290. Manasseh ben Israel campaigned for their return — arguing Jews needed to disperse to all nations before the Second Coming.
p2: Cromwell's Puritan beliefs led him to allow their return so they could be converted to Christianity.
p3: Pragmatic reasons: Jewish financiers would help turn London into a major financial centre; their intelligence networks were also valued.

front: What was the experience of Jewish migrants in the Early Modern period?
p1: 1656: allowed to build their own synagogue; but restricted — forbidden from attending university, serving in the army or becoming lawyers or MPs.
p2: Late 1600s: Jewish community in London had a positive relationship with the mayor and people of the city.
p3: After 1656, Jewish financiers helped turn London into a major financial centre — the first steps toward the City's dominance.

front: How did the experience of black people in England change in the Early Modern period?
p1: Early 1500s: evidence of black Africans living peacefully alongside the English population — racism as a concept had not yet developed.
p2: From the 1560s: Elizabeth I sponsored John Hawkins and Francis Drake in the slave trade; black people began to be seen as property.
p3: 1596: Elizabeth I gave permission for all black people in London to be gathered and sold — though this never actually happened; 1660: Charles II founded the Royal African Company.

front: Why did Palatines come to England?
p1: 1708–09: Wars in the Rhineland region of Germany caused instability; approximately 13,000 Protestant Palatine refugees sought refuge in England.
p2: 1708: Parliament passed the Foreign Protestants Naturalisation Act — offering citizenship to all foreign Protestants; intended for Huguenots but attracted the Palatines.
p3: Palatines saw Protestant England as a safe refuge after years of religious war and instability in Germany.

front: What was the experience of Palatine migrants?
p1: Unlike Huguenots, Palatines were seen as a burden — they lacked specialist skills and arrived in overwhelming numbers.
p2: 3,000 Palatines were deported to Ireland in 1709 when their numbers overwhelmed resources — showed reception depended on economic usefulness.
p3: Reception contrasted sharply with the Huguenots — demonstrated that Protestant faith alone was not enough to guarantee welcome.

front: How did Britain change in the 18th and 19th centuries?
p1: Industrial Revolution: Britain became 'workshop of the world'; huge demand for labour in new industrial port cities.
p2: British Empire conquered ¼ of the globe — increased migration between colonies and Britain.
p3: 1807: Slave Trade abolished; 1833: slavery abolished throughout the British Empire — major shift in the legal status of African and Caribbean migrants.

front: Why did Irish migrants come to Britain in the 1840s?
p1: 1845–46: Potato Blight caused the Great Famine — approximately 2 million fled Ireland; 1 million died.
p2: Ireland lacked industrial cities (outside Belfast) — economic migration to British industrial cities for factory and construction work.
p3: 1820s: restrictions against Catholics lifted in Britain — made it easier for the predominantly Catholic Irish population to migrate legally.

front: What was the experience of Irish migrants?
p1: Worked harsh conditions as 'Navvies' — building Britain's canals and railways. Blamed by the media for diseases and lowering wages.
p2: Anti-Catholic Orange Order resisted Irish Catholic migration; riots in areas of Irish settlement through the 1860s.
p3: Irish Catholics owned only 14% of Irish land due to Protestant Ascendancy — discrimination followed them to Britain.

front: What was the impact of Irish migrants?
p1: Irish Navvies built the rail network connecting all cities and ports in Britain — transformed trade and communication.
p2: Over 20% of Liverpool was Irish — the modern 'Scouse' accent developed from Irish influence.
p3: Irish political leaders like Feargus O'Connor played key roles in the Chartist movement for working-class parliamentary representation.

front: Why did Asian migrants come to Britain in the 18th and 19th centuries?
p1: East India Company developed British trade in India from 1600 — increased travel between India and Britain; first Lascars (Indian sailors) and Ayahs (Indian nannies) arrived.
p2: 1869: Suez Canal opened — increased shipping between Europe and India; greater demand for Lascars on merchant ships.
p3: 1858: Britain took direct control of India after the Indian Rebellion — increased British officials in India employing Ayahs who sometimes returned to Britain.

front: What was the experience of Asian migrants?
p1: Lascars treated poorly by shipping companies — 1876 law gave white sailors 10 feet of personal space and Lascars only 6 feet.
p2: Ayahs often abandoned in Britain after their employers returned home — 1900: Ayahs' Home opened in Hackney to support abandoned Ayahs.
p3: Two Indian (Parsi) migrants became MPs in the 1890s; Queen Victoria was welcoming to migrants — employed Indian advisors.

front: What was the impact of Asian migrants?
p1: Sake Dean Mohamed opened the first curry house in England in 1810 — one of the earliest examples of South Asian cultural impact.
p2: Lascars were essential to British merchant shipping — without them, trade with India and Asia would have been far more expensive.
p3: Growth of new religions: first mosques and Hindu temples built in Britain; Catholicism re-established after centuries of suppression.

front: Case Study: Liverpool in the 19th Century
p1: Liverpool was built on the wealth of the slave trade and became Britain's most cosmopolitan port city.
p2: Over 20% of Liverpool's population was Irish by the mid-19th century — Scouse accent developed from Irish influence.
p3: 1919: race riots broke out at Liverpool docks — Charles Wootton lynched — showing the violent hostility that black port workers faced.

front: How did the experience of black people in Britain change in the 18th and 19th centuries?
p1: 1772: Somerset Case ruled slavery illegal in Britain itself. 1807: Slave Trade abolished. 1833: slavery abolished throughout the British Empire.
p2: 1780s: Black soldiers who had fought for Britain in the American War of Independence were given homes in Britain; Committee for the Relief of the Black Poor (1786) established.
p3: But racist attitudes persisted — black people still treated as status symbols; antisemitic and racist stereotypes visible in popular culture (e.g. Fagin in Oliver Twist).

front: What was the impact of black migrants in the 18th and 19th centuries?
p1: Olaudah Equiano and Ignatius Sancho wrote autobiographies that helped persuade the public and MPs to abolish slavery.
p2: William Cuffay (Caribbean heritage) was a leading figure in the Chartist movement campaigning for working-class parliamentary representation.
