p3: Black migrants helped challenge racist stereotypes through their public presence, writings and political activism.

front: Why did 150,000 Ashkenazi Jews come to Britain in the 1880s?
p1: 1880s: a series of violent pogroms (organised massacres) in the Russian Empire targeted Jewish communities — forced mass flight.
p2: Britain's relative lack of anti-Semitism and greater democracy made it a safe destination.
p3: 1905: Aliens Act — first government restriction on migration — specifically targeted this Jewish influx as 'undesirable'.

front: Case Study: Experience of Ashkenazi Jews in the East End of London
p1: Settled in Whitechapel — pre-existing Sephardic Jewish community helped support new Ashkenazi arrivals.
p2: Faced antisemitic stereotypes; falsely blamed for the Jack the Ripper murders in 1888 due to their presence in Whitechapel.
p3: Jewish migrants founded many successful businesses — Marks and Spencer founded by Jewish migrants; Karl Marx (German-Jewish radical) wrote the Communist Manifesto in London.

front: How did Britain change in the Modern period?
p1: WWI (1914–18) and WWII (1939–45): millions of colonial soldiers from Africa, India and the Caribbean fought for Britain.
p2: Decolonisation of the British Empire led to instability and refugee flows — partition of India/Pakistan (1947) displaced millions.
p3: 1948: British Nationality Act granted citizenship to all subjects of the Empire and Commonwealth — opened migration on a large scale.

front: What was the experience of refugees to Britain?
p1: Belgian refugees in WWI; Polish refugees in WWII — 1947 Polish Resettlement Act allowed those who had served in the British military to remain.
p2: Kindertransport 1930s: Jewish children rescued from Nazi Germany — treated with sympathy as victims of Nazi aggression.
p3: 1951: Britain signed UN Convention on Refugees — allowing asylum seekers to claim refuge; 1981 Nationality Act later made non-white migration more difficult.

front: How did WWI affect migration?
p1: Millions of colonial soldiers from Africa, India and the Caribbean served in the British armed forces.
p2: 'Enemy aliens' (mainly Germans) interned on the Isle of Man.
p3: 1919: race riots broke out in port cities — Cardiff and Liverpool. Charles Wootton lynched in Liverpool docks — showing hostility towards black sailors who had served Britain.

front: How did WWII affect migration?
p1: Millions of colonial soldiers from Africa, India and the Caribbean fought for Britain — increased connection between Britain and the Commonwealth.
p2: Polish and other European refugees settled in Britain; Kindertransport children (mainly Jewish) were welcomed.
p3: Many white Britons resisted American attempts to introduce Jim Crow racial segregation into the UK — showed not all Britons accepted racist policies.

front: Why did the Windrush Generation come to Britain?
p1: Post-WWII: Britain needed rebuilding — huge recruitment drives by London Transport and the NHS in the Caribbean.
p2: 1948: British Nationality Act granted citizenship to all imperial and Commonwealth subjects — legal right to live and work in Britain.
p3: Caribbean economies were struggling; Britain offered employment, higher wages and the chance to contribute to the 'mother country'.

front: How did laws about who could migrate to Britain change in the 20th century?
p1: 1905 Aliens Act: first restriction on migration — targeted 'undesirable' (mainly Jewish) migrants. 1948 British Nationality Act: opened migration from the Empire.
p2: 1962 Commonwealth Immigrants Act limited Commonwealth migration. 1981 Nationality Act made non-white migration harder.
p3: 1992 Maastricht Treaty: free movement of EU citizens to Britain. 2019: Britain left the EU — free movement ended.

front: What was the experience of Windrush migrants?
p1: Colour bars common in housing and employment: 'No Blacks, No Dogs, No Irish' signs. White-dominated trade unions viewed migrants as economic competition.
p2: 1958: race riots in Nottingham and Notting Hill. 1968: Enoch Powell's 'Rivers of Blood' speech — 74% of the public agreed with him.
p3: 2012 Windrush scandal: members of the Windrush Generation unjustly deported after decades of living legally in Britain.

front: How did Windrush migrants impact Britain?
p1: Windrush Generation helped rebuild post-war Britain — by the 1960s, 12% of London Transport employees were from ethnic minorities.
p2: NHS relied on migrants: by 2003, 30% of doctors and 44% of nurses were migrants.
p3: Black migrants introduced new musical genres including jazz, calypso, ska, reggae and grime; 1959: Caribbean Carnival founded by Claudia Jones.

front: How did laws protecting migrants develop in the 20th Century?
p1: 1965 Race Relations Act: banned racial discrimination in public places. 1968 Race Relations Act: extended to housing and employment — outlawing colour bars.
p2: 1971: High Court ruled in favour of the Mangrove Nine. 2005: use of racist language became a hate crime.
p3: 2010 Equalities Act: protection of rights regardless of gender, race, sexuality or religion.

front: What were the anti-immigrant political movements of the 20th century?
p1: 1930s: Oswald Mosley's British Union of Fascists — anti-Semitic movement; defeated at the Battle of Cable Street (1936) when East Londoners blocked their march.
p2: 1967: National Front formed as an anti-immigration party — never won more than 1% of the vote; 1977 Battle of Lewisham — their march resisted by local people.
p3: 2001: riots in Burnley following tensions between white and Asian communities; modern tabloid press frequently scapegoats migrants for social problems.

front: Case Study: Bristol in the mid 20th Century
p1: Bristol Bus Company operated a colour bar — refusing to employ Black or Asian workers.
p2: 1963: Bristol Bus Boycott, organised by the West Indian Development Council and supported by many white students, successfully ended the colour bar.
p3: Guy Bailey was denied a job on the buses due to his race — the boycott directly challenged institutional racism and influenced the 1965 Race Relations Act.

front: Why did East African Asians come to Britain?
p1: 1967: 20,000 Kenyan Asians expelled as part of the 'Africanisation' policy — forced to leave despite holding British citizenship.
p2: 1972: Ugandan dictator Idi Amin expelled all Asians from Uganda — 27,000 came to Britain.
p3: Leicester City Council controversially tried to deter Ugandan Asian migration — in response, many deliberately chose Leicester, which became a major South Asian centre.

front: Case Study: Asian migrants in Leicester
p1: Ugandan and Kenyan Asian migrants settled in Leicester from the 1960s–70s despite initial hostility from the local council.
p2: Belgrave Road became known as the 'Golden Mile' due to the prosperous South Asian businesses and restaurants.
p3: Leicester now hosts the largest Diwali celebrations outside Asia — a transformed multicultural city regenerated by migrant communities.

front: How did Britain's relationship with the European Union change?
p1: 1992: Maastricht Treaty formed the European Union — guaranteed free movement of people between member states.
p2: 2004: eight former communist states (including Poland) joined the EU — large-scale migration to Britain due to stronger British economy.
p3: 2016 Brexit vote; 2019: Britain left the EU — free movement of EU citizens to Britain ended.

front: Why did Windrush Migrants come to Notting Hill in the 1950s?
p1: Caribbean migrants arrived in Britain after the 1948 British Nationality Act — needed cheap accommodation close to work in West London.
p2: Notting Hill had large Victorian houses divided into cheap bedsits by exploitative landlords like Peter Rachman who targeted migrants who had no other options.
p3: Colour bars in housing meant migrants were refused accommodation elsewhere — Notting Hill became a centre of Caribbean settlement by necessity.

front: What was housing like in Notting Hill?
p1: Large Victorian houses subdivided into cramped, expensive bedsits. Landlords like Peter Rachman charged high rents and provided poor conditions.
p2: Colour bars meant Black migrants were refused housing elsewhere — trapped in overcrowded, poor-quality accommodation.
p3: Overcrowding, poor sanitation and exploitation were common — yet migrants had little legal protection and few alternatives.

front: What was the Notting Hill Housing Trust and Pardner schemes?
p1: Notting Hill Housing Trust set up to provide better affordable housing for the Caribbean community — a community response to exploitation by private landlords.
p2: Pardner scheme: a Caribbean savings system where members contributed to a shared pot — each member received the full pot in turn.
p3: Pardner schemes allowed Caribbean migrants to save enough to buy property and start businesses — a self-help system in the absence of bank credit.

front: How did Caribbean culture change Notting Hill?
p1: Caribbean migrants transformed Notting Hill's culture — music, food and community events became central to the area's identity.
p2: 1959: Claudia Jones founded the Caribbean Carnival (forerunner of the Notting Hill Carnival) — a direct response to the 1958 riots, turning community trauma into celebration.
p3: Shebeens, the Mangrove restaurant and the Portobello Road market became key cultural spaces for the Caribbean community.

front: What were Shebeens?
p1: Shebeens were unlicensed clubs run in private houses by Caribbean migrants — provided music, food and drink in a welcoming community space.
p2: Created because mainstream pubs and clubs operated colour bars — Black people were refused entry.
p3: Police regularly raided shebeens — another flashpoint between the Caribbean community and the Metropolitan Police.

front: What was the Portobello Road Market?
p1: Portobello Road Market became a key cultural and commercial space for the Caribbean and broader migrant community in Notting Hill.
p2: Caribbean stalls sold food, music and goods — creating a visible, vibrant presence in the neighbourhood.
p3: The market helped establish Notting Hill as a multicultural area and gave Caribbean traders a space to operate outside mainstream commerce.

front: Why was the Mangrove restaurant important to the Caribbean community?
p1: The Mangrove on All Saints Road was a Caribbean restaurant and community hub run by Frank Crichlow — a gathering place for activists, artists and community members.
p2: Police raided the Mangrove 12 times between 1969 and 1970 despite finding no evidence of wrongdoing — seen as deliberate harassment of the Black community.
p3: 1970: British Black Panthers led by Darcus Howe organised a protest march against the raids — leading directly to the trial of the Mangrove Nine.

front: How did the police treat the black community in Notting Hill?
p1: Metropolitan Police repeatedly stopped and searched Black residents — using the 'sus law' (suspicion of intent to commit a crime) disproportionately against Black people.
p2: Police raided the Mangrove restaurant 12 times (1969–70) and targeted Shebeens — widespread harassment of the Caribbean community.
p3: 1999 Macpherson Report (following Stephen Lawrence's murder) described the Metropolitan Police as 'institutionally racist'.

front: What anti-immigration groups were active in Notting Hill?
p1: The White Defence League and the Ku Klux Klan (British chapter) distributed racist leaflets in Notting Hill in the 1950s.
p2: Teddy Boys were young white men associated with racist violence against Black residents in Notting Hill.
p3: 1967: National Front formed — anti-immigration party that never won significant electoral support but was active in areas like Notting Hill.

front: What happened during the Notting Hill riots (1958)?
p1: August–September 1958: white Teddy Boys and far-right groups launched violent attacks on Black residents over several nights — 'nigger hunting'.
p2: Caribbean community defended itself — some Black residents armed with bottles and iron bars fought back.
p3: Riots shocked the nation but judges gave heavier sentences to Black defendants than white attackers — showing ongoing institutional racism.

front: What happened during and after the murder of Kelso Cochrane (1959)?
p1: May 1959: Kelso Cochrane, a young Antiguan carpenter, was stabbed to death by a gang of white youths in Notting Hill.
p2: Despite witnesses, the murderers were never brought to justice — the case exposed police indifference to racist violence.
p3: Over 1,000 people attended Cochrane's funeral in a powerful demonstration of community solidarity; his death strengthened Caribbean community resolve.

front: How did Claudia Jones change Notting Hill?
p1: Claudia Jones was a Trinidadian-born activist and journalist who founded the West Indian Gazette — the first major Black British newspaper.
p2: 1959: Jones organised the first Caribbean Carnival in a London ballroom — a direct response to the 1958 riots, reclaiming joy from trauma.
p3: Her carnival grew into the Notting Hill Carnival — now the largest street festival in Europe, celebrating Caribbean culture annually.

front: Who were the British Black Panthers?
p1: British Black Panthers formed in the late 1960s — inspired by the American movement; led figures included Darcus Howe and Althea Jones-Lecointe.
p2: Organised the 1970 protest march against police raids on the Mangrove restaurant — directly challenging police harassment.
p3: Darcus Howe was one of the Mangrove Nine who defended himself in court and helped expose police racism — a landmark moment in British civil rights history.

front: Why did the trial of the Mangrove Nine matter?
p1: 1970: Nine Black activists (including Darcus Howe and Frank Crichlow) charged with incitement to riot following the Mangrove protest march.
p2: 1971: all nine acquitted or cleared of most serious charges; the judge acknowledged evidence of police harassment of the Black community — an unprecedented judicial admission.
p3: The trial was a landmark in British civil rights history — exposed institutional racism in the Metropolitan Police and inspired continued activism.

front: What primary sources can we use to find out about Notting Hill?
p1: West Indian Gazette (founded by Claudia Jones, 1958): useful for understanding the Caribbean community's own perspective — reports on discrimination, police harassment, cultural events and the 1958 riots from a Black British viewpoint. Counters the bias of white-owned mainstream press.
p2: Police records (Metropolitan Police): useful for tracking the number of raids on the Mangrove, stop-and-search data, and records of the 1958 riots — but must be treated critically as they reflect police bias and may undercount racist violence against Black residents.
p3: Oral histories: testimonies from named individuals such as Frank Crichlow (Mangrove owner), Darcus Howe (British Black Panthers, Mangrove Nine) and residents who lived through the 1958 riots — useful for personal experience but may be shaped by memory and perspective.
